1:
Henry begins with the change in the form of covenanting. When Israel was first brought into covenant with God it was done by sacrifice and the sprinkling of blood; here it is done by the more natural and common way of sealing and subscribing the written articles, which bound the people to no more than was already their duty. Keil and Delitzsch fix the sense of the opening words against two older readings. The phrase means upon all this, that is, on the foundation of the preceding prayer and penitence, and not after all this, nor in all this evil that had befallen us as Rashi and Aben Ezra took it; and the word for what was made is a settlement or sure agreement rather than a covenant in the sacrificial sense, so that the verb of cutting is used of it only by analogy.

Clarke sets out the order of subscription in four classes, Nehemiah first as their governor, then the priests, then the Levites, then the chiefs of the people. Henry counts them, twenty-two priests, seventeen Levites and forty-four of the chief of the people, and draws the lesson from the order rather than the numbers: those who are above others in dignity and power should go before them in the way of God. He notes too that among the Levites who subscribed were all or most of those who had been the mouth of the congregation in prayer, which showed that they were themselves affected by what they had said and would not bind burdens on others that they declined to touch. Gill says only that these are they who sealed the covenant.

The absence of Ezra from the list is the puzzle of the section, and it draws four different answers. Henry wonders at it, since Ezra had been active in the assembly of the same month and can hardly have been away, and supposes that having already done his part as a scribe he now left it to others to do theirs. Clarke finds it strange without explaining it, and enlarges the difficulty, since neither the high priest Eliashib nor any of the prophets appears either, though some of them must have been at Jerusalem. Wesley proposes an impediment, sickness or something like it, and supports the guess from the later narrative, where Ezra reappears at the dedication of the wall and is evidently free of whatever had hindered him. Ellicott dissolves the problem instead of answering it: the first name is the family name of the high-priestly house to which both Ezra and Eliashib belonged, and one of them, probably Ezra, affixed its seal. He identifies another of the names on the same principle, taking Zidkijah for Zadok the scribe, who was Nehemiah's secretary.

Keil and Delitzsch handle the Levitical names as a matter of record. Fourteen Levites sealed; the sons of two of them had returned with Zerubbabel along with seventy-four others, and four of the names occur elsewhere as heads of orders of Levites. Of the rest nothing further is known, but they may be regarded as heads of Levitical houses. Henry works the same list forward rather than backward, observing that most of those named earlier as heads of houses appear here among the first of the chief of the people, whoever was the present head bearing the name of him who was head when they came out of Babylon, so that these were the fittest to subscribe for their whole father's house.

Clarke closes with a textual note the others do not raise, that the whole of this chapter except its first two verses is wanting in the Arabic version.
8:
Only one voice comments on these two verses, and his notes are short enough to be given whole. On the first Ellicott observes that what the text calls the priests means the names of the priestly families rather than of individual men, and he refers the reader to the fuller priestly list given later in this book for comparison. On the second he does no more than report how far the names can be checked, that five of the Levitical family names are traceable in the earlier registers of the return and in the list of those who came up with Ezra.

What the two notes settle is small but not nothing: the signatories of both orders sign as houses, and a minority of the Levitical houses can be matched against records already in hand. What they leave open is everything else. Ellicott offers no identification of the remaining names, no account of why these particular houses sealed, and no comment on the order in which they stand.
11:
Keil and Delitzsch treat the roll of the chief of the people as a document to be checked against another document rather than as a list of persons. Forty-four names stand under that heading. Thirteen of them are found in the register of the kindreds who came back with Zerubbabel, so that rather less than a third of the signatories can be matched against the returning families by name. The remaining thirty-one they account for in two ways: some are heads of the particular houses into which those larger kindreds were divided, and some are elders of the smaller towns of Benjamin and Judah, which had no kindred name of their own to sign under.

The arithmetic between the two lists is what interests them, and it does not resolve in one direction. The earlier register enumerates thirty-three kindreds and places; this one carries forty-four, which is an increase of eleven. But the increase is not a simple addition, because several names that stand in the earlier list are missing here, Shephatiah and Arah and Zaccai among them, so the later roll is both longer and in places different rather than being the earlier roll with names appended.

Two causes are offered for the difference and neither is made to carry it alone. The first is that a kindred was not a single household: it included several houses, and where that was so the head of each house subscribed separately, which multiplies signatures without multiplying families. The second is that the number of houses had itself grown over the intervening years, so that some of the additional names represent genuinely new units rather than a finer division of old ones. Keil and Delitzsch do not attempt to say how much of the increase belongs to each cause, nor do they explain the disappearance of the names that are absent; the omission of Shephatiah, Arah and Zaccai is left standing as a fact about the list rather than as a problem to be solved. What the account does establish is the kind of list this is. On their reading it is a roll of signing units and not of kindreds, which is why it cannot be set against the earlier register name for name, and why a difference in length between the two carries no conclusion by itself about how many families had returned or remained.
14:
Ellicott is again the only commentator here, and his note is about the kind of list this is rather than about any name in it. The heading covers a mixture: some of the names are personal, some belong to families, some represent places, and some stand independent of any of these, so that the list cannot be read as a roll of individuals or as a roll of clans but must be taken as both at once.

His second observation is comparative. Setting this catalogue beside the register of those who returned from the captivity, he finds that the years between had added to the number of houses. The growth is left as an observation and not pressed into an argument; he does not say how many were added, nor whether the increase came from natural multiplication, from the subdivision of older kindreds, or from families joining the community after the return. Nothing else in the chapter answers the question, and no other voice takes it up.
28:
Who the rest of the people are is answered by subtraction. Gill takes them for those who did not themselves sign and seal; Keil and Delitzsch define them as the members of the community exclusive of the princes and the heads of the priestly and Levitical orders, and suppose that the Nethinim, among whom they count the servants of Solomon, were represented in the assembly by the heads of the Levites. Clarke turns the same fact into a claim about representation, that every one of them had his representative in one or another of the classes that sealed, and that by their sealing they held themselves bound.

The clause about those who had separated themselves is where the section is most often misread, and two of the commentators say so. The natural reading takes them for converts from heathenism, and Ellicott refuses it on three grounds: there is as yet no record of a recognised body of such converts, the word for separated is the same that stands elsewhere in this book with quite another sense, and the verses that follow show the covenant to be concerned precisely with the danger arising out of commerce with the heathen, which would make little sense if the heathen were already inside the assembly. Keil and Delitzsch identify them positively as the descendants of those Israelites who had been left in the land and were now joining the new community, and read the construction as significant in itself, since they are separated from the peoples not merely away from something but toward the law of God, which is to say in order to live by it. On the qualification that follows Ellicott is brief, that children able to take the oath intelligently were included in it.

The act of the people is then described four ways that do not conflict. Gill has them declaring their approbation and ratifying what had been done in their name. Clarke observes that although they did not sign the instrument they bound themselves by a solemn oath to fulfil its conditions. Ellicott calls it a union of the people as such, springing from a deep national conviction. Wesley presses the social point hardest: the commonalty agreed with their nobles, and great men never look so great as when they encourage religion and are examples of it, nor can they secure the regard of the best of their inferiors by anything more surely; and he notes that the nobles are here called their brethren, since in the things of God rich and poor meet together. On the curse and the oath Ellicott distinguishes the two instruments precisely, the oath assuming the obligation and the curse imprecating the penalty of violation.

The first two undertakings are handled briskly. Gill reads the marriage clause against the history, that they had intermarried already, were prone to it, and did it again after this. Clarke reduces it to a phrase, that they would make no affinity with the people of the land. On the sabbath Gill glosses the word for ware as anything that could be sold and carried away; Clarke states the two resolutions plainly, that the sabbath should be kept and that the land should have its own rest every seventh year; and Ellicott extends the first to the great festivals equally with the weekly rest, takes the sabbatical year as following naturally with the ground left untilled, and identifies the last clause with the release of debts belonging to that year. Wesley adds the reason for singling this commandment out, that the profanation of the sabbath is a sure inlet to all manner of profaneness.
32:
Gill notices first what kind of thing this is: an ordinance the people made among themselves, binding them to what the law of God had not bound them to. Keil and Delitzsch qualify that sharply. The payment is in their view a revival of the Mosaic precept that every man of twenty years and upwards should give half a shekel, a tribute still being paid in the gospel period; what is new is only the rate, lowered to a third of a shekel in consideration of the poverty of the greater part of the community. They reject the view of Aben Ezra that the third was an addition to the half rather than a reduction of it, as unsupported by the text, and note that the text does not say who was liable, which they take as evidence that the custom was already well known. They also restrict the term for service to the regular worship rather than to the building and repair of the temple.

Henry approaches the same fund from the side of necessity. There had formerly been treasures in the house of the Lord for this charge and they were gone, with no settled fund in their place; the table and altar were a constant expense, and they had no rich king to provide as Hezekiah had, while the priests' own maintenance was too small to bear it. So the people charged themselves, and he makes the arithmetic the moral: when every one will act and every one will give, though but little, the whole amount will be considerable. He is careful that the governor did not impose the tax but that the people made it an ordinance for themselves.

The wood offering draws the fullest comment, because the law had provided for the fire without providing for the fuel. Keil and Delitzsch state the gap exactly: the law prescribes that wood be kept burning on the altar and that the priest burn wood on it every morning, but gives no direction about procuring it, so the rulers must always have made some arrangement. Clarke supplies a historical reason why an arrangement was needed now. Fetching wood had been the business of the Nethinim, the hewers of wood and drawers of water, and after the captivity few of them were to be found, since as descendants of the Gibeonites they were reckoned little better than slaves and had as much interest in staying where they were as in returning. With too few of them left, the lot was cast, and Clarke is precise that it did not decide who should furnish the wood but which class or district should furnish it at which season, so that the supply should be continuous.

What the practice became afterwards is added by two of them. Clarke reports that the bringing of the wood grew into a great day and was constituted a feast, which Josephus names as the carrying of the wood, and remarks that it is not mentioned in the sacred writings because while the Nethinim were numerous there was no occasion for it. Ellicott says the same more briefly, finding here the origin of the feast of the wood offering, a single day afterwards substituted for the appointed times through the year, and adds that the lot determined the order in which the classes supplied it. Gill notes only how the lot was drawn, the priests and Levites together in one and the people in another.
35:
Ellicott marks a change of construction at the head of this section: what follows hangs on the ordinance made earlier and not on the casting of lots, and the very minuteness with which each due is specified implies to him that neglect had crept in, the law having turned an expression of natural piety into an obligation. Gill makes the same separation from the other side, that these things were undertaken by oath rather than settled by lot, and reports the narrower opinion of Aben Ezra, who confines the term to the sheaf and the two wave loaves.

The dues themselves fall into two classes which the chapter is careful to keep apart, and Keil and Delitzsch set out the whole arrangement once: the earliest yield of ground and orchard; sons redeemed at the priest's valuation; unclean beasts redeemed in the same way; and the young of herd and flock, whose fat went up on the altar while the flesh fell to the ministers. They notice that the grammar shifts here from the infinitive to the first person, so that a description of what was owed becomes a promise to render it. Ellicott fastens on the pairing that this produces, sons standing beside animals exactly as they do elsewhere in the law, where the beasts so paired are expressly the unclean ones; money bought back both, while the clean young went to the altar. Gill identifies those unclean beasts as the ass and its kind. Clarke reaches behind the whole institution for its reason, that every eldest son belonged to God by right and that the tribe of Levi was accepted in their room, which is why Levites and not eldest sons served at the sanctuary.

What follows is a chain with a check built into it. Clarke describes the links: a tenth of the produce of the fields went to Levi, and a tenth of that tenth to Aaron. Ellicott explains why a priest had to stand by while the country collections were made, namely to see that his own order's share was secured before the remainder travelled up to Jerusalem; he identifies the storerooms as those described in the account of the first temple, to which a treasury for this purpose was added later, and glosses the towns of tillage as farming places where produce was first gathered in. Gill puts the same safeguard in terms of character rather than machinery: someone was always present to observe what came in, so that the collectors should be neither tempted nor suspected. Keil and Delitzsch read the last sentence of the chapter as confirming what precedes, since the whole community carried its offerings to the same rooms.

The pledge at the end is read against what came after it. Ellicott observes drily that both the promise and its breach are accounted for by a later chapter of this same book. Clarke takes the sentence as a text instead of a clause, builds from it an account of the house of God with its family, its officers, its worship and its means of support, and closes by turning the questions on the reader: whether he belongs to that household, what place in it he holds, whether he keeps to its ordinances, and whether he has forsaken it.
